title: Aid programmes used as cover for spies
conviction: Four cases are on the public record, each exposed by accident. Whether the practice continues is the suspicion.
story: In 2011 a Pakistani doctor named Shakil Afridi went door to door in the town of Abbottabad offering hepatitis B vaccinations. The drive was run for the CIA, which was trying to find out who was living in the walled compound where Osama bin Laden was hiding. Afterwards the deans of US public health schools wrote that seven or more United Nations workers vaccinating Pakistani children against polio had been shot dead, and in May 2014 the White House promised that the CIA would make no operational use of vaccination programmes, a promise that covers vaccination and nothing else. The suspicion this entry describes is that Abbottabad was not a one-off: that rich governments have used their aid programmes, over and over, as cover for intelligence work and political operations inside other countries. If so, people who accept a vaccine, a police-training course or a new building from a foreign aid agency cannot know who is really behind it, and the danger falls on genuine aid workers.

The record goes back decades. From 1962 to 1974 the US aid agency, USAID, ran an Office of Public Safety that trained and equipped police abroad. Its director from 1962 to 1973, Byron Engle, is described in published histories as a CIA operative. By one historical count it sent about 1,500 advisers to at least 52 countries, and Congress ended it in 1974 after Senator James Abourezk set out to expose its activities amid accusations that it taught torture. Forty years later, in 2014, the Associated Press revealed that USAID had built ZunZuneo, a text-message network for Cubans, through front companies in Spain and the Cayman Islands, paid through foreign banks. By USAID's own count it had about 68,000 users before it shut down in September 2012, and they were not told who had made it. USAID said the programme was not covert.

Other governments have done the same. In 2004 Australia's foreign intelligence service, ASIS, placed listening devices in the walls of Timor-Leste's cabinet offices in Dili while they were being renovated under an Australian aid project, during negotiations over oil and gas in the Timor Sea. That case is told in full in the entry on spying at the negotiating table. Each of these came out by accident: congressional pressure in one, more than 1,000 pages of documents obtained by reporters in another, a retired spy's complaint in the third. The 1974 law that banned US training of foreign police had gained 'a dozen exemptions' by 1992, according to Senator Alan Cranston, whose remarks the Federation of American Scientists reproduces with a GAO report. No law in the United States or Australia requires the government to say whether intelligence officers work under aid cover today.

The question would be settled by the CIA's own records of how it used aid cover after 1974, the files the USAID inspector general opened on ZunZuneo in 2014, the records on ZunZuneo that the Senate Foreign Relations Committee demanded from USAID that year, and Australia's records of the aid project in Dili. If those show that the known cases were the whole of it, the suspicion fails.
missing: No count exists of intelligence use of aid cover after 1974. The USAID inspector general's 2014 file and the Senate Foreign Relations Committee records have not been located in published form.
would_settle: Declassified CIA records on use of aid cover after 1974; the USAID inspector general's 2014 ZunZuneo review; the records the Senate Foreign Relations Committee requested from USAID on ZunZuneo in 2014.

title: Forecasts inflated so countries borrow more
conviction: An insider's account, the World Bank's own 1992 review, a 245-dam study and an IMF working paper all find forecasts biased upward. Whether the bias is deliberate is the suspicion.
story: In 1971 a young economist named John Perkins went to work for Chas. T. Main, an engineering firm in Boston, and by his own account rose to be its chief economist. In a 2004 book, Confessions of an Economic Hit Man, he wrote that his real job had been to produce inflated growth forecasts, so that countries would take large loans for power and infrastructure projects built by US companies and be left owing more than they could pay. Critics disputed many of his claims, above all that the National Security Agency was involved in hiring him. Einar Greve, the vice-president who hired him, at first backed the book's general account and later denied parts of it, including any link to the NSA. The suspicion this entry describes does not depend on Perkins: it is that the forecasts behind big loans are pushed upward on purpose, costs written low and benefits written high, so the loan gets approved and the contractors get paid, and the borrowing country carries the debt when the numbers never arrive.

The World Bank's own review points the same way. In 1992 its Wapenhans report found that 37.5 per cent of the Bank's projects completed in 1991 were judged failures, up from 15 per cent in 1981. It blamed an "approval culture" in which staff treated project appraisals as a way to win approval, and found a growing bias toward over-optimistic expected returns.

So do other studies. In 2014 an Oxford team, Atif Ansar, Bent Flyvbjerg and colleagues, studied 245 large dams in 65 countries built between 1934 and 2007. On average the dams cost 96 per cent more than budgeted, three in four ran over, and Ansar told International Rivers that dams backed by development banks did no better. The study names deliberate underestimating to win approval as one of the root causes. In 2020 an IMF working paper found the Fund's own growth forecasts too optimistic by about 0.2 percentage points a year, adding up to about one point over five years, and more optimistic the deeper the budget cuts the programme planned. On this map, the Yacyretá dam between Paraguay and Argentina saw its cost rise from $2.5 billion to over $10.5 billion, or over $15 billion by International Rivers' count.

An honest mistake and a deliberate one leave the same trace in a forecast, so the missing piece is intent. It would show in the working files: appraisal models and consultants' forecasts for large loan-financed projects, read beside the drafts they replaced and the outcomes that followed. The World Bank's evaluation office says the inside history of the 1992 task force is documented in the Bank's archives, and a count of how often forecasts were raised under deadline pressure would test whether the bias was pushed or simply drifted.
missing: No study has compared draft and final appraisal forecasts across the Bank's portfolio.
would_settle: Appraisal models and consultant forecasts for large loan-financed projects, compared draft against final and against outcomes, starting from the Portfolio Management Task Force files in the World Bank archives.

title: Lenders kept funding dictators they knew were stealing
conviction: Two leaked internal documents show lenders knew of large-scale theft; lending continued in both cases. How often this happened is the suspicion.
story: In 1982 a confidential report by a retired German central banker leaked from Zaire, now the Democratic Republic of Congo. Erwin Blumenthal had been sent by the IMF to run the country's central bank, and on Zaire's $4.1 billion foreign debt he wrote that there was "no - I repeat no - chance" the creditors would be repaid, because of the corruption of the people in power. The lending did not stop. Probe International counted that over the next six years the IMF lent Zaire $600 million, the World Bank $650 million and Western governments nearly $3 billion, and when Mobutu Sese Seko was overthrown in 1997 the country owed more than $13 billion. The suspicion is that this was a habit, not an accident: that the big lenders often knew the governments they lent to were stealing, kept lending because those governments were useful allies, and then held ordinary people responsible for the debt.

Indonesia under Suharto is the second case on paper. In August 1997 World Bank staff in Jakarta wrote a confidential memo estimating that at least 20 to 30 per cent of the government's development budget was diverted through informal payments to officials and politicians, that there was no basis to claim Bank projects lost less, and that there were reports of 50 to 80 per cent being taken from money meant for land purchase and resettlement. The month before, the Bank's vice-president for East Asia, Jean-Michel Severino, had said the Bank knew exactly where its money was going. The memo became public only when the Wall Street Journal obtained it in 1998.

The Philippines shows who pays. Under Ferdinand Marcos, Westinghouse built the Bataan nuclear plant, which cost about $2.3 billion, was finished in 1984 and never produced electricity. Westinghouse admitted paying $17.2 million to a Marcos associate, Herminio Disini, which it called a legitimate commission, and a US jury acquitted the company of bribery in 1993. In 2021 the Philippine Supreme Court held Disini liable for using undue influence to win Westinghouse the contract. Filipinos finished paying the plant's loans in April 2007, a total of 64.7 billion pesos in principal and interest. There is an old idea in international law, odious debt, that debts a regime takes on against its own people should not bind them, but it has rarely been applied.

Lenders do not have to publish what their staff knew when a loan was approved, and the two documents above surfaced only through leaks. What would settle the suspicion are the internal country risk assessments and board papers for lending to Zaire, Indonesia and the Philippines in those years, and to other long-ruling allies, many of which are now old enough to request from the lenders' archives.
missing: No systematic review of lender archives for internal warnings of theft before continued lending.
would_settle: Internal country risk assessments and board papers for lending to Zaire, Indonesia and the Philippines in the 1970s to 1990s, requested from the World Bank and IMF archives.

countries.note: Blumenthal report 1982; lending continued; debt over $13 billion by 1997.

title: Aid money turns up in Swiss bank accounts
conviction: One peer-reviewed study, partly by a World Bank economist, measures the leak. Who moved the money, and why the Bank held the paper, are the suspicion.
story: In February 2020 a professor in Copenhagen, Niels Johannesen, posted a research paper on his own website. He had written it with Jørgen Juel Andersen and the World Bank's own economist Bob Rijkers, comparing World Bank aid payments to the 22 most aid-dependent countries with bank deposits recorded by the Bank for International Settlements. In the quarters when a country received aid worth 1 per cent of its national income, its deposits in offshore centres known for bank secrecy rose by 3.4 per cent, while its deposits in ordinary financial centres did not move, so that about 7.5 per cent of the aid appeared to leak out, with the rise driven by accounts in Switzerland and Luxembourg. The Economist reported that the paper had passed the Bank's internal review in November 2019 but that higher officials blocked publication, and linked the resignation of the Bank's chief economist, Pinelopi Goldberg, after less than 15 months, to the paper. Within hours of Johannesen posting it, the Bank published it; it later passed peer review in the Journal of Political Economy. The suspicion is that a steady slice of the money lent and given to the poorest countries ends up in the private accounts of the people who run them, and that the lenders would rather not count it.

An older line of research found the same thing in loans. The economists Léonce Ndikumana and James Boyce estimated capital flight from 33 sub-Saharan African countries between 1970 and 2004 at $443 billion in 2004 dollars, against foreign debts of $195 billion, which makes the region a net creditor to the rest of the world. In their analysis, roughly 60 cents of every dollar borrowed abroad left again as capital flight in the same year. In their book Africa's Odious Debts they write that a significant part ended up in private accounts at the same banks that had made the loans. On this map, the documented pattern on investment routed through tax havens shows how companies use the same havens.

Neither study can say whose money it was. Both rest on country totals, Swiss and other haven banks do not publish who holds their accounts, and no public record traces where a disbursement went after it reached a government's account. That is why the evidence is statistical rather than a list of names.

What would settle it is account-level information: records from the haven banks of deposits from officials in the weeks after aid or loans were paid out, which tax authorities can now obtain under information-exchange treaties. Two further records would help: the Bank's internal correspondence on why the 2020 paper was held, and the same test run on IMF lending, regional development banks and individual donor governments.
missing: The same method has not been applied to IMF, regional bank or bilateral donor disbursements. No account-level records are public.
would_settle: Account-level haven deposit records matched to disbursement dates; the World Bank's internal correspondence on the paper's review; the method rerun on other lenders.

countries.note: By far the most important haven among those with country-level data; with Luxembourg, drove the rise.
Highest aid-to-GDP ratio in the study's sample (33.5 per cent), per ProMarket.

title: Rescue loans that rescue the banks, not the country
conviction: Leaked IMF board minutes and a line-by-line study of where the Greek money went. Whether rescues are designed this way as a rule is the suspicion.
story: On 9 May 2010 the IMF's board met in Washington to approve its share of a €110 billion rescue for Greece, behind minutes marked strictly confidential. When they reached the Wall Street Journal in 2013, they showed Brazil's director warning that the programme might be seen not as a rescue of Greece but as a bailout of Greece's private debt holders, mainly European financial institutions, and directors for Argentina, Brazil, India, Russia and Switzerland saying it lacked any cut in Greece's debt to private lenders. The Dutch, French and German directors told the board their banks would broadly keep their Greek bonds; according to The Press Project, banks from those three countries held more than $122 billion of them early in 2010 and began selling that spring. A 2016 study by the European School of Management and Technology in Berlin found that of €215.9 billion paid out in Greece's first two programmes, less than 5 per cent went into the Greek budget for anything other than old debts, interest and bank rescues, though its authors also blamed years of high Greek spending. On this map, the 2012 Greek programme cut the minimum wage by 22 per cent, and other cards record the protests that followed. The suspicion is that big rescue loans are designed first to pay foreign private lenders back in full, moving their losses onto the borrowing country's taxpayers, while the country gets years of cuts.

Mexico in 1995 had the same shape. In 1994 the Mexican government had sold short-term bonds called tesobonos, paid in pesos but tied to the value of the dollar, and the amount outstanding grew from $3.1 billion in March to $29.2 billion in December, about $17 billion of it held by foreign investors. When the peso collapsed that December, the United States put together a rescue of about $50 billion, including $20 billion from the US Treasury and $17.8 billion from the IMF, which let Mexico pay the bonds as they fell due. Critics in Washington called it a bailout of Wall Street investors in Mexican bonds. Mexico repaid the US loans early, with interest, and the Clinton administration called it a success.

In Mexico the bondholders were paid what they were owed, and the public lenders who replaced them were then repaid by Mexico. Who held the bonds at the moment of each rescue is rarely published, which is what makes it hard to say whose losses were avoided.

What would settle the question are the full IMF staff papers behind the 2010 Greek programme, the European Central Bank's records of which Greek bonds it bought and from whom, the month-by-month exposure reports of the named banks in 2010, and a list of who held Mexico's tesobonos in January 1995. Together they would show whether these rescues were shaped around getting particular creditors out before the losses fell.
missing: The ECB's bond-purchase counterparty records and month-by-month bank exposure data for 2010 have not been obtained.
would_settle: Full IMF staff papers for the 2010 Greek arrangement; ECB records of Greek bond purchases by counterparty; month-by-month 2010 exposure reports of the French, German and Dutch banks.

title: The lenders expect the riots their conditions cause
conviction: A leaked World Bank strategy, a count of 146 protests and a global study linking adjustment loans to repression. Whether the lenders plan for repression is the suspicion.
story: On 25 June 2024 Kenya's parliament passed a finance bill full of new taxes, and protesters forced their way into the parliament building. Police opened fire. Kenya's state-funded human rights commission later said police had killed at least 60 people. Human Rights Watch reported that the bill was meant to raise an extra $2.3 billion, in part to meet IMF revenue requirements. The suspicion is that the lenders know, before they set conditions like these, that prices will rise, people will protest and governments will use force, and that they write this into their plans as an acceptable cost.

There is a paper trail. In 2001 Joseph Stiglitz, a former World Bank chief economist, described the "IMF riot" to the reporter Greg Palast as one of the steps of a lending programme. Palast's team at the Observer and the BBC obtained confidential World Bank documents, among them an interim strategy for Ecuador which said, more than once, that the plans could be expected to spark social unrest, and which called for meeting it with political resolve.

Researchers have counted what follows. In their 1994 book Free Markets and Food Riots, John Walton and David Seddon listed 146 protests against austerity in 39 debtor countries between 1976 and 1992. A global study by Rodwan Abouharb and David Cingranelli covering 1981 to 2000, which allowed for the fact that troubled countries are more likely to get such loans in the first place, found that carrying out a World Bank structural adjustment agreement worsened governments' respect for freedom from torture, political imprisonment, killings by the state and disappearances. This map holds cases of the same shape: the Caracazo in Venezuela in 1989, where the card counts 276 dead after fuel prices rose, and Ecuador in October 2019, where ending fuel subsidies more than doubled prices and 11 people died. The documented pattern on this map, the money kept flowing after the killings, shows that the lending usually continued.

The planning documents are usually confidential, and the Ecuador strategy came out through a leak. Lenders do not count deaths that follow their programmes. What would settle the question is a count across published IMF staff reports and World Bank programme documents of how often the risk sections predicted unrest before a big price rise, and whether the plan changed when they did. Many of those documents are now public after the fact, so the count can be done.
missing: No count of risk sections in IMF and World Bank programme documents that forecast unrest.
would_settle: A count of IMF staff reports and World Bank programme documents whose risk sections forecast unrest before major price increases, with whether the programme changed.

countries.note: At least 60 killed by police, per the national human rights commission.

title: Global rankings bent for countries with money to give
conviction: A law firm's investigation found the rankings were changed for China and Saudi Arabia. Whether this was routine is the suspicion.
story: In 2017 Kristalina Georgieva, then chief executive of the World Bank, went to the home of a manager on the Bank's Doing Business team to collect a printed copy of the final report, and thanked the employee for helping to resolve the problem. That is one detail from an investigation by the law firm WilmerHale, published in September 2021, which found that staff had changed China's data under pressure from the office of the Bank's president, Jim Yong Kim, and from Georgieva, at a time when the Bank was seeking China's support for a large increase in its capital. The changes put China at 78th in the 2018 edition, seven places higher than the draft data had it. Georgieva said she disagreed fundamentally with the findings, and the IMF's board, where she had become managing director, backed her in October 2021. Doing Business ranked 190 countries on how easy they made it to start and run a company; investors used it and governments rewrote laws to climb it. The suspicion is that global rankings like this are bent for countries the institution needs or that pay it, and that the scoring itself pushed countries to strip protections from workers.

China was not the only case. For the 2020 edition, WilmerHale found that senior staff changed Saudi Arabia's data. Saudi Arabia rose 30 places to 62nd and was named the top improver, and it had paid the Bank for advisory work aimed at improving the very indicators being scored. In 2006 Saudi Arabia's king had said he wanted the country among the top ten by 2010. WilmerHale found no evidence that the president's office or the board were involved in the 2020 changes. The Bank cancelled Doing Business.

There had been warnings. In January 2018 the Bank's chief economist, Paul Romer, said Chile had fallen in the rankings because of changes in method rather than in Chile, and suggested politics might be behind it. He then said he had not meant to suggest manipulation, and resigned; Augusto Lopez-Claros, who had directed the group that published the rankings, called the claim that the changes targeted Chile wholly without merit. The rankings also shaped laws. Until 2009 they scored countries higher for weaker worker protections, through what was called the employing workers indicator. The Bank suspended that indicator in 2009 after pressure from unions, the International Labour Organization and the US Congress, and an independent panel the Bank set up in 2013 recommended removing it permanently.

WilmerHale examined two editions. What would settle whether China and Saudi Arabia were exceptions is the full record of original and final data for every country in every edition from 2003, with each change and who asked for it. The Bank's new Business Ready ranking, launched in 2024, brings a labour topic back, so the same record matters again.
missing: The full data change log across all Doing Business editions has not been published.
would_settle: Original and final data for every country in every Doing Business edition, 2003 to 2020, with each change and its requester.

title: Secret loans arranged by banks and traders, kept from the public
conviction: A bank's guilty plea, debts revealed overnight in Congo and Chad, and $385 billion of underreported Chinese-linked debt. That hidden lending is routine is the suspicion.
story: In the port of Maputo, Mozambique, a fleet of tuna boats bought with borrowed money has sat rusting for years. In 2013 and 2014 three companies linked to Mozambique's state borrowed about $2 billion through Credit Suisse and Russia's VTB for the fleet and for coastal security, and the loans were taken without the approval of Mozambique's parliament, with more than $1 billion of them kept secret from the IMF until 2016. The Financial Times reported that the deals had been inflated from $300 million to over $2 billion. US authorities said about $200 million went in bribes and kickbacks, about $150 million of it to Mozambican officials and about $50 million to Credit Suisse bankers. In 2021 Credit Suisse admitted fraud, agreed to pay about $475 million to US and UK authorities, and cancelled $200 million of Mozambique's debt. A study by Mozambique's Centre for Public Integrity and Norway's Chr. Michelsen Institute put the cost to the economy at $11 billion and found the slowdown pushed nearly two million people into poverty. The suspicion is that this is not unusual: that arranging hidden loans is ordinary business for some international banks and commodity traders, and that the public finds out only when the country can no longer pay.

Commodity traders make hidden loans too. In the Republic of Congo, Glencore and Trafigura had lent the government money to be repaid in future oil. In 2017 the IMF raised its estimate of Congo's debt from 77 to 110 per cent of national income after hidden debts came to light; Debt Justice said it could not tell how much of the jump was hidden debt and how much was falling output or new loans. Global Witness later found the state oil company carrying up to $3.3 billion more that had never been disclosed. In Chad, Glencore held 98 per cent of the government's foreign commercial debt by the end of 2016, and in 2016 $231 million of the government's $271 million in net oil revenue, about 85 per cent, went to Glencore.

The same thing happens with Chinese lending and in Europe. In 2021 AidData found about $385 billion of debt linked to Chinese lending that poorer governments had not reported, mostly because it was owed by state companies and special-purpose firms rather than the government itself. In Europe, Goldman Sachs arranged currency swaps for Greece in 2001 that hid about €2.8 billion of debt, after Greece had joined the euro; Goldman said the swaps were legal under the rules of the time.

These debts stay hidden because the World Bank's debt register relies on what governments choose to report, loans to state companies are often left out, and trader prepayment deals are private contracts. AidData found the size of the gap for Chinese lending by comparing what lenders recorded with what borrowers reported. Nobody has done the same for Western banks and commodity traders, and doing so country by country would show how much of the world's debt is missing from the official numbers.
missing: No creditor-side comparison has been made for Western banks and commodity traders as AidData did for Chinese lenders.
would_settle: A country-by-country comparison of creditor-side records (bank and trader filings, BIS data) with debtor reports to the World Bank Debtor Reporting System.

title: Rescue money timed to keep friendly governments in power
conviction: Three rescues arrived just before elections, with one US official's reported admission and one president's public condition. Whether this is a regular practice is the suspicion.
story: In February 1996 the IMF agreed a $10.2 billion loan to Boris Yeltsin's government in Russia, four months before Yeltsin faced the Communist candidate, Gennady Zyuganov, in a presidential election in which he was trailing in the polls. The IMF's managing director said the Fund was not taking sides; Zyuganov called the loan political. That summer The Economist claimed that the IMF and the Russian government had worked together to keep Russia within the loan conditions on paper, and once Yeltsin had won, the IMF held back a payment. The suspicion is that the biggest powers behind the lenders time and size rescue money to keep friendly governments in office. If so, voters in borrowing countries are choosing under pressure they may not see.

Argentina has been through it twice. In June 2018 the IMF approved the largest loan in its history for the government of Mauricio Macri, raised in October to $57 billion, equal to 1,227 per cent of Argentina's quota at the Fund, a year before Macri ran for re-election. In July 2020 Mauricio Claver-Carone, Donald Trump's adviser on Latin America, was reported to have told a teleconference held by the Chilean Council on Foreign Relations that Trump asked the IMF for the loan so that Macri would win; Argentine senators repeated the account in a letter that November. The IMF's own 2021 review found the programme did not meet its objectives, only four of its twelve planned reviews were completed, and Macri lost. On 14 October 2025, twelve days before Argentina's midterm elections, Trump sat beside President Javier Milei at the White House, talked about the $20 billion the US Treasury had just made available, and said: "If he loses, we are not going to be generous with Argentina." His Treasury Secretary, Scott Bessent, said the support was tied to policy, not to the election. Milei's party won about 41 per cent of the vote.

Researchers have measured the tilt. A study of 157 countries from 1999 to 2005 by the economist Axel Dreher and colleagues found that countries voting with the United States at the UN General Assembly received lower inflation forecasts from the IMF as their elections approached. This map's documented pattern on aid and UN votes shows the same pull on aid.

The instructions that the US Treasury gives its director on the IMF board are not published, and board minutes are confidential for years. What would settle the question are those instructions and minutes for the 1996 and 2018 loans, and a count across all IMF programmes of approvals and payments in the months before elections, set against how closely each government votes with the largest shareholders.

would_settle: US Treasury voting instructions and IMF board minutes for the 1996 Russian and 2018 Argentine arrangements; a count of pre-election approvals and disbursements across all IMF programmes by voting alignment.

title: Chinese-financed ports that may be future naval bases
conviction: One base opened after years of denial, a second facility hosting Chinese warships, and a researched shortlist of eight more. That port lending is laying the ground for bases is the suspicion.
story: For years China said it had no plans for a military base in Djibouti, on the Horn of Africa. It confirmed one in November 2015 and opened it in 2017. The suspicion is that some of the ports China has paid for or built around the world were planned with a second purpose: places where its navy could dock, refuel and one day be based, with the loans giving Beijing the leverage to ask. If so, a country taking a Chinese loan for a harbour may also be signing up, without saying so, to a side in a future conflict.

Cambodia's Ream naval base is the case being watched. In 2019 the Wall Street Journal reported an agreement giving China's navy use of the base for 30 years; both governments denied it. China paid to rebuild Ream, and satellite images showed a new pier almost identical to the one at Djibouti and long enough to berth Chinese aircraft carriers. Two Chinese warships berthed there from December 2023. Cambodia formally opened the rebuilt Ream in April 2025 and declared it open to foreign navies, and a US warship visited in early 2026. In 2023 AidData counted 123 Chinese-financed seaport projects at 78 ports in 46 countries, worth $29.9 billion, and named the eight most likely places for China's next bases: Hambantota in Sri Lanka, Bata in Equatorial Guinea, Gwadar in Pakistan, Kribi in Cameroon, Ream, Luganville in Vanuatu, Nacala in Mozambique and Nouakchott in Mauritania. It also noted that none of them is currently militarily defensible.

One famous version of this story does not hold. Hambantota is often described as a port China seized when Sri Lanka could not pay. Research for Chatham House found otherwise: the 2017 99-year lease to China Merchants Port was a new investment of $1.12 billion, not a swap of debt for the port, the Chinese loans for the port were only 4.8 per cent of the government's foreign debt, and Sri Lanka got no debt relief from it. So the suspicion is not a debt trap. It is that commercial ports are being chosen and built so they can serve a navy too. On this map, Hambantota's industrial zone met protests over the taking of village and farm land, and Gwadar's port and new expressway have pushed fishers off their homes and fishing routes.

The port contracts and loan agreements are mostly unpublished, which is where any clause giving warships access would sit. What would settle the question is publication of those contracts, and the records of which naval vessels call at the eight shortlisted ports over the coming years. Repeated long stays by Chinese warships would confirm the suspicion; their absence would weaken it.
missing: Port concession and loan contracts for the eight shortlisted ports are unpublished; no consolidated log of naval port calls.
would_settle: Publication of the concession and loan contracts for the shortlisted ports; naval port-call records for those ports over time.

title: Poor countries chosen to take rich countries' toxic waste
conviction: A World Bank memo set out the logic and a commodity trader's ship followed it. Whether waste flows follow that logic as a rule is the suspicion.
story: On the night of 19 August 2006, lorries began dumping black liquid at rubbish tips and roadsides around Abidjan, the largest city in Côte d'Ivoire. It was more than 500 tonnes of waste from the Probo Koala, a ship chartered by the oil trader Trafigura, which had tried to unload it in Amsterdam that July and taken it back on board. In Abidjan a newly licensed local firm, Compagnie Tommy, was hired to get rid of it for about $17,000. More than 100,000 people sought medical help; a national inquiry recorded 15 deaths and an Ivorian court 17. Trafigura paid the government about $198 million in 2007 in a settlement that ended prosecution, and £30 million in 2009 to about 30,000 people who had sued in London, both without admitting liability, and a Dutch court fined it €1 million in 2010 for concealing how dangerous the waste was. Trafigura has always said the waste could not have caused deaths or serious injury. The suspicion is that companies, and some of the economists who advise the big lenders, treat people in poor countries as cheaper to poison, and that hazardous waste travels to where harming people costs least.

The logic had been written down at the World Bank. A memo dated 12 December 1991 went out under the name of Lawrence Summers, then the Bank's chief economist. It argued that health-damaging pollution should be done where its cost was lowest, which meant the country with the lowest wages, and it called the economic logic of dumping a load of toxic waste in the lowest-wage country "impeccable". The memo was actually written by a Bank economist, Lant Pritchett. Both men said it was meant as sarcasm, and Pritchett said the leaked version had been doctored to remove context. Friends of the Earth leaked it in February 1992 to the Brazilian newspaper Jornal do Brasil, and Brazil's environment secretary, José Lutzenberger, replied that the reasoning was logical and insane.

The trade it describes has a long record. In 1987 and 1988 two Italian firms arranged to store about 18,000 drums of hazardous waste in the Nigerian port of Koko, paying a local man about $100 a month for the use of his yard; the drums leaked, Nigeria forced Italy to take them back, and the scandal helped bring about the Basel Convention on hazardous waste in 1989. When China stopped accepting plastic waste for recycling at the start of 2018, exports from rich countries moved to Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam and Indonesia, where illegal plants burned plastic in the open; Malaysia, Indonesia and the Philippines later shipped containers of contaminated waste back to the countries that had sent them.

Shipments like these are often hidden by calling waste something else, such as a ship's slops, building materials or goods for recycling. Countries that have signed the Basel Convention report their exports each year. Matching those reports against the wages and the waste-treatment capacity of the countries receiving the waste would show whether the trade follows the memo's logic or not.
missing: No analysis matching Basel Convention export reports to destination wages and treatment capacity.
would_settle: Basel Convention national reports on hazardous waste exports, matched to destination-country wages and treatment capacity.

title: Markets forced open for rich countries' subsidized food
conviction: A former US president's apology, a reversed tariff in Ghana and the collapse of local farming in both. Whether lending conditions are written for rich-country exporters is the suspicion.
story: In March 2010, two months after the earthquake that destroyed much of Port-au-Prince, Bill Clinton told the US Senate that a policy he had pushed in Haiti in the 1990s had been a mistake. "It may have been good for some of my farmers in Arkansas," he said, but it had cost Haiti its ability to grow its own rice. In 1995, under a programme run with the IMF and the World Bank, Haiti had cut its tariff on imported rice to 3 per cent, a year after Clinton restored President Jean-Bertrand Aristide to power. Haiti now buys more than 80 per cent of its rice from the United States, and between 1995 and 2011, according to the Environmental Working Group, Arkansas farmers received more than $2 billion in direct federal payments, half of it for rice. The suspicion is that conditions telling poor countries to cut tariffs on food imports were written to open markets for farm exporters in rich countries, whose governments pay them large subsidies, and that local farmers paid the price.

Ghana tells the same story with chickens. Imports of chicken rose from 26,000 tonnes in 2002 to about 40,000 tonnes in 2004, and local farmers' share of their own market fell from 95 per cent in 1992 to 11 per cent in 2002. In 2003 Ghana's parliament voted to double the tariff on imported poultry to 40 per cent. The government backed down within two months, under pressure from the IMF according to press reports, and Inter Press Service reported that the European Union's trade commissioner, Pascal Lamy, had lobbied against the tariff. The EU pays its own farmers about €43 billion a year.

Food aid follows the same direction. The long-running US food aid programme Food for Peace requires that the food it sends be grown in the United States, so emergency help sent through it is bought from American farmers and shipped. This map's documented pattern on tied aid shows how much aid money goes back to companies in the donor country.

The loan conditions are public; the reasons behind them are not. What would settle the question is a country-by-country comparison of the food-tariff cuts written into IMF and World Bank programmes with which rich countries' exporters gained market share afterwards, read beside the negotiating records, such as the instructions the US and EU gave their directors on those programmes.
missing: No country-by-country comparison of lender-required tariff cuts with subsequent export gains by rich-country suppliers.
would_settle: Food-tariff conditions in IMF and World Bank programmes matched to post-programme import shares by supplier country, read with US and EU instructions to their executive directors.

countries.note: Tariff cut to 3 per cent in 1995; over 80 per cent of rice now from the US.

title: Carbon credits driving a new land grab
conviction: Agreements covering a fifth of Zimbabwe and a tenth of Liberia and Zambia, a court ruling against Kenya's largest soil-carbon project, and evictions rights groups have linked to carbon deals. That carbon finance is driving evictions is the suspicion.
story: On 2 November 2023, the Kenyan government began evicting the Ogiek, an Indigenous people who have lived in the Mau Forest for generations, from their homes at Sasimwani. Survival International counted about 167 houses destroyed, including a school. A few weeks earlier Kenya had signed an agreement with a Dubai company, Blue Carbon, to produce carbon credits on millions of hectares. Amnesty International, Minority Rights Group and Survival International put out a joint statement asking whether carbon credits were behind the evictions. The government said it was protecting the environment, and Blue Carbon told the BBC it had no ongoing projects in Kenya. The suspicion is that the market in carbon credits, which lets companies pay for forests to be protected so they can count that against their own emissions, is driving a new land grab in poor countries, in which governments sign huge areas over to foreign firms and the people living there are fenced out.

Blue Carbon was set up in 2022 and is chaired by a member of Dubai's ruling family, Sheikh Ahmed Dalmook Al Maktoum. During 2023 it signed agreements covering about a fifth of Zimbabwe (7.5 million hectares), about a tenth of Zambia (8 million hectares), 8 million hectares of Tanzania's forest reserves and about a tenth of Liberia (around 1 million hectares), altogether an area about the size of the United Kingdom. Under the leaked Liberian agreement, the company would take 70 per cent of the income for the first ten years. Liberia's government later said its deal had been stopped, and an AFP investigation in 2025 found that other deals had also gone nowhere.

Where carbon projects have gone ahead, a court and the main certifier have found problems. In northern Kenya, the Northern Rangelands Trust runs a soil-carbon project covering more than 2 million hectares across 14 community conservancies, selling credits to companies including Netflix and Meta. In January 2025 a Kenyan court ruled that two of its largest conservancies had been set up unconstitutionally, with no basis in law; one of them produced about a fifth of the project's credits. Verra, the main body that certifies carbon credits, suspended the project in 2023 and again in 2025, and reinstated it in 2026. This map holds earlier cases of the same kind: the Sengwer evicted from Embobut Forest in 2014, and carbon projects in Peru, Cambodia, Kenya and the Democratic Republic of Congo.

Most carbon agreements between governments and companies are not published, and Liberia's became known only because it leaked. What would settle the question is the full set of carbon-rights agreements signed since 2020, together with the registries of certified projects, checked against court records and documented evictions in the same areas. A count of how many registered land-based carbon projects overlap with evictions would show whether the cases here are exceptions or the pattern.
missing: No count of registered land-based carbon projects overlapping documented evictions.
would_settle: All government carbon-rights agreements since 2020 and carbon registry project boundaries, checked against court records and documented evictions.

title: Loans cut off to bring down governments the West dislikes
conviction: Declassified notes, congressional records and freedom-of-information documents show lending stopped for political reasons in Chile, Nicaragua and Haiti. That this is a standing weapon is the suspicion.
story: On 15 September 1970, eleven days after Salvador Allende won Chile's presidential election, President Richard Nixon met the CIA's director, Richard Helms, in the White House. Helms's handwritten notes of the meeting, declassified in 1975 during a Senate investigation, include the instruction to make the economy scream. In the years that followed, the World Bank made no new loans to Chile, and the Senate investigation found that loans from the Inter-American Development Bank fell from $46 million in 1970 to $2 million in 1972. After the 1973 coup that brought General Augusto Pinochet to power, World Bank loans flowed again. Historians still argue over how much the cut-off itself hurt Chile, since the IMF kept lending and some older loans kept paying out. The suspicion is that cutting off lending through the banks the West controls is a standing weapon, used to weaken governments the United States dislikes, in ways voters in the target country never see as a decision.

Nicaragua in the 1980s is the second case. After the Sandinistas came to power, the United States opposed their loan requests at the World Bank and the Inter-American Development Bank. In January 1985 the US Secretary of State, George Shultz, wrote to the president of the Inter-American Development Bank warning against a proposed $58 million loan to Nicaragua and raising future US funding for the bank. Several of the bank's member governments criticized the letter at the bank's annual meeting that March, and the Heritage Foundation reported that the bank approved no new loans for Nicaragua after 1983.

Haiti in 2001 is the third. The Inter-American Development Bank had approved four loans worth $146 million for health, drinking water, roads and education in Haiti between 1996 and 1998. After Jean-Bertrand Aristide's party won elections in 2000, the money was not paid out. On 6 April 2001 the US executive director at the bank, Lawrence Harrington, wrote to its president asking that the loans not be paid out, and the Robert F. Kennedy Memorial Center, which later obtained Treasury documents through freedom-of-information requests and a lawsuit, says the bank's about-face followed. A 2003 Congressional Research Service report also listed disputes over the 2000 elections, Haiti's arrears to the bank and unmet loan conditions as reasons the money was held up. Haiti's water system went without the money while the bank, according to press reports, still asked Haiti to pay arrears; in July 2003 Haiti paid $32 million to clear them, leaving about $3 million in its reserves.

Most of what passes between the US Treasury and its directors at the development banks is never published, and the RFK Center had to go to court to get some of it. What would settle the question is the full set of US instructions to its directors on loans to governments it opposed, and a count of how often approved or pending loans stalled after elections the United States did not like.
missing: No count of loans stalled after elections the US opposed; Treasury instructions to its directors largely unreleased.
would_settle: US Treasury instructions to its executive directors at the World Bank and IDB on loans to governments it opposed, and a count of stalled loans after disfavoured election results.

title: Spying on poor countries to win resource and trade deals
conviction: Australia's bugging of Timor-Leste's cabinet was exposed by the intelligence officer who led it, who later pleaded guilty to revealing secret information, and was followed by a renegotiated treaty, though Australia has never officially confirmed it; the Snowden files show spying on G20 delegates and Brazil's state oil company. That rich governments routinely spy to win economic deals is the suspicion.
story: In 2004 a team from Australia's foreign intelligence service, ASIS, placed listening devices in the walls of Timor-Leste's cabinet offices in Dili, which were being renovated under an Australian aid project. Timor-Leste was one of the poorest countries in the region, two years independent, and it was negotiating with Australia over how to share the oil and gas of the Timor Sea, including the Greater Sunrise fields. ABC's Lateline reported that transcripts of the bugged conversations were delivered to Australia's negotiating team. The treaty signed in 2006 split Greater Sunrise's revenue evenly and set no permanent border. The operation came out years later through a former ASIS officer, known only as Witness K. Timor-Leste took Australia to arbitration in The Hague in 2013, and in 2018 the two countries signed a new treaty setting a maritime boundary. Witness K pleaded guilty to conspiring to reveal secret information and received a suspended sentence; the prosecution of his lawyer, Bernard Collaery, was dropped in July 2022. The suspicion is that rich governments routinely spy on poorer ones to win resource and trade deals, and that the deals people later live under were negotiated by one side that could hear the other's plans.

The Snowden files show the same thing at larger meetings. In 2013 the Guardian reported documents showing that Britain's signals intelligence agency, GCHQ, had intercepted the phones and computers of delegates at the G20 meetings in London in 2009, including by setting up internet cafes for them, and had passed what it gathered to British ministers. Among the targets it named was the Turkish finance minister. The same year Brazil's TV Globo reported documents showing that the US National Security Agency had targeted Petrobras, Brazil's state oil company, through a programme that extracts data from private networks. Brazil's president, Dilma Rousseff, said that if confirmed it could only be for economic and strategic reasons.
Spying of this kind is generally authorized under the spying country's own law, so it is rarely tried in that country's courts, and the people who reveal it are often the ones prosecuted.

What would settle how common it is are the intelligence agencies' records of operations against trade, debt and resource negotiations, which only a leak or a court order is likely to produce. Short of that, a count of negotiations later reopened or challenged on the ground of spying, as Timor-Leste did, would show whether the known cases are rare or merely the ones that surfaced.
missing: No count of trade, debt or resource negotiations reopened on espionage grounds.
would_settle: Intelligence records of operations against economic negotiations, obtained by leak or court order; a count of negotiations reopened or challenged on espionage grounds.

title: Bribes built into the contracts that loans pay for
conviction: Court convictions in Lesotho and a record settlement by Siemens show bribery on lender-financed contracts. That bribes are a routine cost built into such contracts, and passed on to borrowers, is the suspicion.
story: Between 1988 and 1998 Masupha Sole, the chief executive of the Lesotho Highlands Water Project, a set of dams sending water from the mountains of Lesotho to Johannesburg, took about $2 million in bribes paid through middlemen on behalf of 12 international construction and engineering firms. Some of the money went into his Swiss bank accounts. The World Bank lent to the project. Lesotho, one of the world's poorest countries, prosecuted: Sole was sentenced to 18 years, reduced to 15 on appeal, and the Canadian firm Acres International and the German firm Lahmeyer International were convicted. The World Bank barred Acres from its contracts for three years in 2004 and Lahmeyer for seven in 2006, and critics said the Bank had moved slowly. The suspicion is that bribery is a routine cost of winning contracts paid for by development loans, built into the price, and that the borrowing country repays the loan, bribe included.

Siemens, the German engineering company, showed how routine it could be. In December 2008 it agreed to pay about $1.6 billion in fines and penalties in the United States and Germany. The US Securities and Exchange Commission said it had made 4,283 separate payments totalling about $1.4 billion to bribe officials around the world between 2001 and 2007. A US official described bribery at the company as standard operating procedure. In a separate settlement with the World Bank, Siemens agreed to spend $100 million over 15 years on anti-corruption work and to stay out of Bank business for two years, after a Russian subsidiary was found to have engaged in corrupt practices on a Bank-financed transport project in Moscow.

Companies are caught when a borrowing government is willing to prosecute, when a rich country's regulator acts, as the United States did with Siemens, or when the World Bank's own investigators find the evidence, as they did with Siemens's Russian subsidiary. The World Bank's debarment list records only the firms that were caught.

What would settle how common this is are the full investigation files behind the World Bank's debarments, and a comparison of prices on lender-financed contracts with the prices the same firms charged for similar work elsewhere. A consistent premium on financed contracts would show the cost being passed on to borrowers.
missing: No price comparison between lender-financed contracts and comparable unfinanced work by the same firms.
would_settle: World Bank debarment investigation files; a price comparison of lender-financed contracts against comparable work by the same firms.

title: Aid money used to win arms sales
conviction: A British court ruled aid for Malaysia's Pergau dam unlawful amid a linked arms deal, and BAE paid Tanzania £29.5 million after an overpriced military radar sale. That aid budgets are bent to sell weapons is the suspicion.
story: On 10 November 1994 the High Court in London ruled that the British government had acted unlawfully when it gave £234 million of aid to build the Pergau dam in Malaysia. The case was brought by the campaign group World Development Movement, which argued the dam was so uneconomic that it could not count as development. Behind it lay an arms deal: Margaret Thatcher had promised help with the dam in 1989 while Britain was negotiating a £1.3 billion sale of weapons to Malaysia, and officials told a parliamentary committee that the arms deal would have been lost without the aid promise. The suspicion is that aid budgets are regularly bent to win weapons and other large contracts for the donor country's companies, so that money given in the name of the poor ends up paying for deals that serve the donor's industry.

Tanzania shows the other direction of the same trade. In a deal agreed in 1999 and cleared for export by Britain in 2001, the British arms company BAE Systems sold Tanzania, one of the world's poorest countries and a large recipient of British aid, a military radar system for about £28 million to use for civil air traffic control. The World Bank and the International Civil Aviation Organization said it was too expensive and unsuited to the job, and Britain's development secretary, Clare Short, delayed a £10 million aid payment and suggested the deal was corrupt. Investigators later found that BAE had paid about $12 million to a marketing adviser; the case never established where the money went after that. In 2010 BAE pleaded guilty in Britain only to an accounting offence and agreed to pay £29.5 million, which was paid in 2012 for textbooks and other school supplies in Tanzania.

The radar deal came to court only through a fraud investigation, and the 2010 plea agreement ended it with an accounting offence, so the bribery allegations were never tested at trial. The same aid ministries that give money to poor countries sit inside governments that promote their own arms and engineering exporters, and the record of how those interests are weighed against each other is rarely published.

What would settle how common this is are the internal files linking aid offers to export deals in donor governments, starting with the ones released in Britain's own Pergau inquiry, and a count, donor by donor, of how often large aid packages coincided with arms or major equipment sales to the same country.
missing: No donor-by-donor count of large aid packages coinciding with arms or major equipment sales.
would_settle: Donor government files linking aid offers to export deals; a count of large aid packages coinciding with arms sales to the same country.

title: Foreign advisers who profit from the privatisations they design
conviction: A US court found Harvard's lead advisers on Russia's privatisation liable for investing on the side; the loans-for-shares auctions are widely described as rigged. That advisers and insiders routinely profit from sell-offs they shape is the suspicion.
story: In December 1992 the US aid agency, USAID, hired the Harvard Institute for International Development to advise Boris Yeltsin's government on turning Russia's state economy into a market one, a contract eventually worth tens of millions of dollars. The project's leaders, the Harvard economist Andrei Shleifer and the lawyer Jonathan Hay, were meant to be neutral advisers. In 2004 a US federal judge found both liable under the US False Claims Act for making personal investments in Russia while advising on its markets, including shares in Russian oil companies held in the name of Shleifer's father-in-law. In 2005 Harvard paid $26.5 million to settle, Shleifer agreed to pay $2 million and Hay up to $2 million, none of them admitting liability, and the institute had already been dissolved. The suspicion is that the foreign advisers and favoured insiders who design the sale of a country's public assets routinely position themselves to profit from it, so that the advice is shaped by who will buy.

Russia's next large sell-off went to insiders. In November and December 1995 the government ran the loans-for-shares auctions, in which stakes in 12 large state companies, including Norilsk Nickel and the oil company Yukos, were pledged to banks in return for loans to the state. The banks that ran the auctions won most of them, usually for bids just above the starting price; 51 per cent of the voting shares in Norilsk Nickel went for about $170 million and 45 per cent of Yukos for about $159 million. Contemporary reports described the auctions as rigged, and the scheme gave several of the men later called the oligarchs control of major companies. Some economists, such as Daniel Treisman, argue that the companies were later run better than comparable state firms. On this map, a Lancet study links Russia's mass privatisation to a sharp rise in deaths among working-age men.

The advisers' own investments came out after American whistle-blowers in Moscow complained and the US government sued. Advisory contracts on privatisation are usually confidential, and there is no public register of what the advisers, their firms or their families hold in the companies being sold.

What would settle it is a comparison, for large privatisations financed or advised by foreign lenders, of who designed the sale against who bought into it, using the advisory contracts and the shareholder registers that followed. If advisers and their associates turn up among the buyers more often than chance, the suspicion holds.
missing: No comparison of privatisation advisers against later shareholders across lender-advised sales.
would_settle: Advisory contracts for large lender-advised privatisations matched against subsequent shareholder registers.

title: Seed laws pushed on poor countries that restrict farmers' own seed
conviction: The World Bank's own agriculture rankings scored seed laws, and its loans have required seed certification laws as conditions. That this serves seed companies at farmers' expense is the suspicion.
story: In 2016 the World Bank held up Tanzania as a model for having joined the 1991 version of the UPOV Convention, an international treaty that protects the rights of those who breed new plant varieties. Under Tanzania's seed laws, farmers who save, swap or sell protected seed, as their families have done for generations, can face fines or prison. The praise came in a new World Bank ranking, Enabling the Business of Agriculture, which the Bank launched in 2013 at the request of the G8 group of rich countries to score how well each country's laws suited agribusiness. The suspicion is that the lenders are using rankings and loan conditions to rewrite seed laws across Africa and Asia for the benefit of a handful of large seed and chemical companies, and against the farmers who supply most of their own seed.

The rankings were backed by loan conditions. The aid agency CAFOD went through 15 years of World Bank documents and found two requirements that countries had to meet before receiving agricultural loans: subsidies tied to buying hybrid seed and the fertiliser that goes with it, in Mali, Niger, Kenya and Guinea between 2017 and 2020, and seed certification laws that limit what small farmers can grow, save, share and sell, in the Central African Republic, Chad, Ghana, Sierra Leone, Liberia, Mozambique and Nigeria. CAFOD notes that across Africa farmers' own seed systems supply about 80 per cent of the seed they plant. In 2017, 157 organisations and academics signed a statement against the ranking's seed scoring, and the Oakland Institute reported that it had already inspired a new seed ordinance in Rwanda opening the way to UPOV.

The Bank says its seed indicators measure laws and rules that support the timely release of new seed to farmers and acknowledges that farmers also use informal seed. But a ranking that scores only the formal seed market, and a loan that requires certification laws, push in one direction, and six Western firms control over two-thirds of the world's commercial seed sales, according to the Oakland Institute. Who asked for each seed condition, and who drafted the laws that followed, is not part of the published loan documents.

What would settle it is the drafting history of the seed laws passed after these loans and rankings, including which consultants and companies were involved, and a count of how far the share of certified seed bought from foreign companies rose in the countries that changed their laws.
missing: No drafting history of post-loan seed laws; no count of foreign seed-company market share before and after.
would_settle: Drafting records of seed laws passed after World Bank conditions or rankings; certified-seed market shares by supplier before and after.

title: Pension funds and university endowments behind land grabs
conviction: In a preliminary report, Brazil's land agency found that land deals involving a US pension manager broke limits on foreign ownership, and a Brazilian court froze the deed to land held by Harvard's endowment; research groups link the farms to land grabbing and deforestation. That ordinary people's savings are financing land grabs worldwide is the suspicion.
story: In the Matopiba region of Brazil's Cerrado, the world's most biodiverse savannah, some of the farms that took over land from traditional communities after 2008 were bought with the retirement savings of American university teachers and with Harvard University's endowment. Research by the Brazilian network Rede Social and the group GRAIN found that Harvard's endowment had spent more than $1 billion over a decade on about 850,000 hectares of farmland on five continents, nearly 300,000 hectares of it in the Cerrado, while Chain Reaction Research reported that the pension manager TIAA had bought at least 13 farms in Matopiba, at least four from companies associated with a man known in the region for illegal land grabbing. Both funds have been linked to deforestation and fires on their land. In a preliminary report revealed in December 2020, Brazil's land agency, Incra, found that TIAA's indirect part in land bought by a Brazilian company it co-owns broke Brazil's limits on foreign land ownership, which TIAA disputes; in October 2020 a Bahia state court froze the deed to a 107,000-hectare tract held by Harvard's Brazilian company and reopened an inquiry into whether it was public land illegally transferred to private hands. The suspicion is that the savings of ordinary people in rich countries, held by pension funds and endowments, are financing land grabs and forest clearing across the world, out of sight of the people whose money it is.

The rush began after the financial crash of 2008, when pension funds, endowments and private equity looked for assets that would hold their value, and farmland was one. In 2015 GRAIN and Rede Social reported that Sweden's national pension fund AP2 and two Canadian pension funds, the Caisse de dépôt et placement du Québec and British Columbia's bcIMC, had put money into a global farmland fund that bought Brazilian farms through a structure of companies and debentures which, the groups said, let them evade Brazil's limits on foreign land ownership; the fund's manager said the farms were bought legally. In parts of the Cerrado, GRAIN reports, false land titles are commonly used to claim public land before it is sold on.

The funds say they apply strict standards and that some problems predate their purchases. But the savers and institutions whose money pays for these farms are generally not told which farms they own, and the corporate layers make it hard even for researchers to know.

What would settle how far this reaches is a full list of the farmland held by the largest pension funds and endowments, by country and by farm, checked against land registries, deforestation maps and records of evictions. Such lists exist inside the funds and are not published.
missing: No public farm-level list of pension fund and endowment farmland holdings.
would_settle: Farm-level farmland holdings of the largest pension funds and endowments, checked against land registries, deforestation data and eviction records.

title: Development money that flows through tax havens
conviction: Oxfam found most of the World Bank's private-sector lending in sub-Saharan Africa went to companies using tax havens. That development lenders are helping the companies they fund avoid the taxes the countries need is the suspicion.
story: In April 2016, days after the Panama Papers broke, Oxfam published an analysis of the companies that the International Finance Corporation, the World Bank's lending arm for private business, had funded in sub-Saharan Africa in 2015. Of the 68 companies, 51 used tax havens in ways that had no apparent link to their business, and together they received 84 per cent of the money the IFC put into the region that year. Mauritius was the most common haven, involved in 40 per cent of the IFC's projects in the region. The IFC's investments in companies using havens had more than doubled in five years, from $1.2 billion in 2010 to $2.87 billion in 2015. The suspicion is that the development lenders, whose stated purpose is to help poor countries raise their own money, are funding the very corporate structures that drain those countries of tax.

This map's documented pattern on investment routed through tax havens records UNCTAD's estimate that developing countries lose about $100 billion a year in tax on investment linked to offshore hubs, and the IMF economists' finding that almost 40 per cent of global foreign direct investment passes through empty companies, mostly in ten economies including Mauritius. Senegal ended its tax treaty with Mauritius in 2020, saying it had cost $257 million in lost revenue.

The IFC said in response that there are legitimate uses for offshore structures and that it requires the companies it funds to comply with tax law. But the IFC does not publish how much tax its clients pay in the countries where they operate, and its disclosure rules do not require clients to show it, so whether the havens are being used to cut tax cannot be checked from outside.

What would settle it is country-by-country reporting of profits and taxes paid by every company that development lenders fund, set beside where those companies are incorporated. If the companies booking profits in havens pay markedly less tax in the countries where they operate, the suspicion holds.
missing: No country-by-country tax reporting for development-lender clients.
would_settle: Country-by-country profit and tax reporting by all companies funded by development lenders, compared by place of incorporation.
